title: Decision Models in Agentic Architectures: From Production to Agent Skills
gist: Aletyx co-founder Alex Porcelli argues enterprise AI's core problem isn't inconsistency but lack of accountability, and demonstrates wiring deterministic DMN decision models (via Drools) into LLM agents as skills and NVIDIA NeMo guardrails so high-stakes decisions stay auditable, versioned, and business-owned while still using AI for interaction and orchestration.

themes.theme: The accountability gap in enterprise AI

insights.claim: Porcelli argues that non-determinism itself is not the core problem in enterprise AI — it's a symptom — and the deeper issue is lack of accountability: the ability to reproduce a decision, explain why input A and input B produced output C (grounded in policy/regulation), and govern and version that decision-making process over time.
insights.speaker: Alex Porcelli
insights.so_what: Reframes the enterprise AI adoption bottleneck from 'model quality/consistency' to 'auditability infrastructure' — investors should value AI governance/traceability tooling as a distinct, durable category rather than expecting better models alone to unlock regulated-industry adoption.
insights.quote: The major problem that I see on this landscape is not the consistency alone but is the lack of accountability.
insights.locator: I want to highlight two elements

insights.claim: Porcelli cites Mark Cuban's observation that the biggest current challenge for enterprise AI is that it's still impossible to guarantee everyone gets the same answer to the same question every time, and links this directly to why domain knowledge and judgment become more valuable as AI capability increases.
insights.speaker: Alex Porcelli
insights.so_what: Supports a thesis that domain-expert labor is not commoditized by AI but complementary to it — investment implication: tools/roles that encode and audit domain judgment (not just raw LLM access) capture disproportionate value.
insights.quote: I'm coming to the conclusion that the biggest challenge for enterprise AI and AI in general, as of now, is that it's still impossible to make sure that everyone gets the same answer to the same question, every time.
insights.locator: reading this post from Mark Cuban

insights.claim: Porcelli contends that generating code with AI (instead of letting AI make the decision directly) reduces non-determinism but does not solve accountability, because code mixes control flow, infrastructure, and business rules together, making it hard to trace decisions back to the governing policy regardless of whether a human or AI wrote it.
insights.speaker: Alex Porcelli
insights.so_what: Challenges the common 'just have AI write code, not make decisions' mitigation pattern — implies that code-generation-centric AI coding tools are insufficient for regulated high-stakes decision logic, favoring dedicated decision-model layers instead.
insights.quote: Code by itself is a mix of different things. There are control flow, infrastructure, and business rules all mixed in.
insights.locator: You may say that your Python code will be committed

themes.theme: Decision models (DMN/Drools) as the deterministic layer

insights.claim: Decision models are proposed as valuable only for a minority of decisions — specifically high-stakes ones like loan approval or insurance claims processing — not for routine daily interactions, distinguishing where deterministic governance is worth the overhead.
insights.speaker: Alex Porcelli
insights.so_what: Gives investors/architects a sizing heuristic: deterministic decision-model tooling addresses a bounded, high-value slice of enterprise AI (regulated/high-stakes decisions), not general-purpose AI interaction — informs TAM estimates for vendors like Aletyx.
insights.locator: I'm not saying this is valuable for every decision

insights.claim: A real client data pipeline reclassifying customers processes 20 million transactions using this decision-model technology at 18,000 transactions per second, completing the full reclassification in under 20 minutes.
insights.speaker: Alex Porcelli
insights.so_what: Concrete throughput benchmark (18K TPS) for DMN/Drools-based decisioning at enterprise scale — useful for evaluating whether deterministic rule engines can keep pace with high-volume AI-adjacent pipelines versus LLM-based classification.
insights.quote: This technology processes 18,000 transactions per second, so they process everything under 20 minutes.
insights.locator: This is real data from one of our clients

insights.claim: DMN (Decision Model Notation) is an open specification, and decision models built in it can be processed by the open-source Drools engine, meaning the underlying decision logic is portable and not vendor-locked to Aletyx's tooling.
insights.speaker: Alex Porcelli
insights.so_what: Open-standard, open-source foundation lowers vendor lock-in risk for enterprises adopting decision-model governance, and signals Aletyx's moat is likely in tooling/UX/integration rather than the core execution engine.
insights.quote: This is an open specification. This is called DMN, decision model notation. You can use this open source software to process this type of models. The open-source project, Drools.
insights.locator: What I'm presenting here is not something that I created

insights.claim: Because decision models are deterministic and define their entire logic universe explicitly, they cannot hallucinate or deviate — this places them in a different branch of AI ('symbolic AI' from expert systems), distinct from LLM-based generation, and expert-system-derived decisioning has already been deployed in enterprises for over 20 years.
insights.speaker: Alex Porcelli
insights.so_what: Positions symbolic AI/rules engines as a complementary, non-hallucinating counterpart to LLMs rather than a legacy technology to be replaced — relevant for portfolio construction across 'old AI' (rules/expert systems) versus 'new AI' (LLM) vendors.
insights.quote: The decision model is a deterministic thing. You define all the universe within there and it will not hallucinate.
insights.locator: How do you catch hallucinations then?

insights.claim: If an agent asks a decision model to classify an input outside its defined scope (missing or faulty data), the model fails to execute and returns a failure rather than fabricating an answer — analogous to how a coding agent's grep or curl call fails cleanly rather than inventing output.
insights.speaker: Alex Porcelli
insights.so_what: Fail-closed behavior at the tool layer is a concrete architectural safeguard against silent AI errors in high-stakes workflows — a differentiator over pure LLM decisioning, which tends to answer confidently even when wrong.
insights.quote: It will not make up any data. That's the whole point of this.
insights.locator: What happens, this time, is it will return that something was not possible to execute

themes.theme: AI-generated decision models and agent skills workflow

insights.claim: Aletyx's workflow lets AI convert an uploaded business spreadsheet (the format domain experts already use for rules) directly into an executable DMN decision-table model, translating tacit business logic into a governed, auditable format without requiring the business user to learn a new modeling tool.
insights.speaker: Alex Porcelli
insights.so_what: Spreadsheet-to-decision-model AI conversion is a concrete productized wedge for capturing dispersed 'shadow business logic' living in spreadsheets across large enterprises — a scalable go-to-market angle for decision-governance vendors.
insights.locator: I will upload that spreadsheet and ask for an AI

insights.claim: Once a decision model is published, the system automatically generates a Skill.md file and REST endpoints so an AI agent can discover and invoke the model as a domain-specific 'agent skill' rather than a generic tool, with every execution traced back to the specific model version for full input/output audit.
insights.speaker: Alex Porcelli
insights.so_what: Demonstrates a concrete pattern for converting deterministic business logic into the emerging 'agent skills' ecosystem — early architecture reference for enterprises building auditable agentic systems, relevant to any agent-tooling investment thesis.
insights.quote: Every information was traced. With that, we can go back to the model in that version and see the inputs and the outputs and go back to the whole tree of the model.
insights.locator: What I saw is that based on the expressiveness of this model

insights.claim: In a live demo, the agent ('Kairos') using the generated skill correctly classified two different customer profiles (AAA for a US $100k/45-year-old, BBC for a Brazilian equivalent), matching the underlying decision table exactly, illustrating that deterministic model execution constrains the agent's otherwise variable output.
insights.speaker: Alex Porcelli
insights.so_what: Live proof-of-concept that skill-wrapped deterministic models produce consistent classification outcomes across repeated agent interactions — evidence the approach works in practice, not just in theory.
insights.locator: Demo - Wire a Decision Model into NVIDIA NeMo

insights.claim: The AI-driven model-generation process (spreadsheet-to-DMN, or model-to-skill) is itself non-deterministic because it mixes the company's own models with frontier LLMs, meaning only the resulting decision model's execution is deterministic, not its creation.
insights.speaker: Alex Porcelli
insights.so_what: Important nuance for due diligence: determinism guarantees apply only downstream of model authoring — the authoring step still requires human review/testing before deployment, limiting full automation claims.
insights.quote: It's not deterministic, for the reason that we mix our own models with frontier models. It is a mix.
insights.locator: Did you notice that it's deterministic, it always followed the graph?

themes.theme: NVIDIA NeMo as a deterministic guardrail layer

insights.claim: Porcelli demonstrated wiring a decision model directly into NVIDIA NeMo as a guardrail: a YAML skill specification generates Colang rails that intercept LLM inputs/outputs and delegate to the deterministic decision model when triggered, without requiring the agent skill layer at all.
insights.speaker: Alex Porcelli
insights.so_what: Shows a second integration pattern (middleware/guardrail-level, not just agent-skill-level) for injecting deterministic governance into any LLM pipeline — relevant to evaluating NVIDIA NeMo's ecosystem role in enterprise AI governance stacks.
insights.locator: Demo - Wire a Decision Model into NVIDIA NeMo as a Guardrail

insights.claim: In a live demo, an unguarded LLM asked to classify an 18-year-old with $29,000 income returned 'BBB' when prompted to bias toward AAA, but activating the NeMo guardrail tied to the decision model produced the correct deterministic classification instead, demonstrating the guardrail overriding a confidently wrong (and manipulable) LLM answer.
insights.speaker: Alex Porcelli
insights.so_what: Concrete demonstration that ungoverned LLMs are susceptible to prompt-based steering toward incorrect high-stakes outputs, and that deterministic guardrails can neutralize this — a security/compliance argument for guardrail adoption in regulated LLM deployments.
insights.quote: The first answer was very convincing. This is precise. This is what it was supposed to be.
insights.locator: I'm trying to play with the AI, say, I'm a CEO

insights.claim: Porcelli's key takeaway is that isolating business logic into decision models shifts ownership of high-stakes decision logic to the business side, while IT's role becomes governance (testing changes at volume, ensuring no regression) rather than authoring or gatekeeping the logic itself.
insights.speaker: Alex Porcelli
insights.so_what: Predicts an organizational shift in enterprises adopting this pattern: business/compliance teams gain direct control over decision logic, IT becomes a governance/testing function — relevant for evaluating headcount and tooling budget shifts inside large regulated enterprises.
insights.quote: IT becomes part of the governance process... Who owns the decision models, ended up being the business side.

insights.claim: Porcelli argues that existing robotic process automation (RPA) only captures form data entry but does not delegate actual judgment, and that AI's real opportunity in enterprise workflows (e.g., a bank branch employee manually retyping 100-field forms) is to handle ambiguity, ask clarifying questions, and make the decision itself — provided accountability is solved.
insights.speaker: Alex Porcelli
insights.so_what: Reframes RPA as a limited, soon-superseded automation layer versus accountable agentic decisioning — a bearish signal for legacy RPA vendors that don't add decision-governance capability, and a bullish one for accountable-agent tooling.
insights.quote: There is already a technology that does that. It's robotic process automation... We can do much better, and that is why AI can enable that.
